newsitem.title: USA: NYC comptroller says gov's budget penalizes city.
newsitem.headline: NYC comptroller says gov's budget penalizes city.

text.p: New York City's comptroller on Tuesday criticized Gov. George Pataki's proposed budget for fiscal 1998, saying it penalized the city by making it absorb too many spending reductions and cost containment measures.

Saying the state budget should be evenhanded, Alan Hevesi, in prepared remarks, said: "The governor's executive budget, however, proposes large reductions in state aid for essential city higher education and health programs that support regional economic development."

"Moreover, it once again fails to rectfy the most important imbalance in state funding formulas: the city gets less aid than its share of school children," added the city comptroller, a Democrat who decided not to challenge New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani in the November election.

Hevesi, who released a report analyzing the Republican governor's budget in four areas, calculated that downstate gets $3.3 billion less from Albany than it contributes. Long Island's two counties, Nassau and Suffolk, as well as three counties just north of the city, Westchester, Rockland and Putnam, make up the downstate region.
Some of the reports findings follow:

--NYC, which has 37.2 percent of the public school students in the state, only gets 34.7 percent of state deucation aid under the gov's proposed budget--less than the 34.8 percent share it got in fiscal 1997. Giving the city its proportional share would mean another $264 million for the Board of Education. The amount spent per student fell to $6,952 in fiscal 1997 from $7,444 in fisal 1994.
--New York State owed the city about $712 million for outstanding education claims from 1989 to 1996, and the new budget only earmarks $9 million for paying them.

--Albany spends 15 percent of its budget on Medicaid--and 67 percent of that sum in the city--but the program would be cut $1.6 billion under Pataki's plan. For every $1 the city saves in Medicaid reductions, its health care economy loses $4. The governor's proposed cuts, combined with city and federal reductions, would cost providers almost $1.7 billion, while the city would lose $133.6 million in taxes.

Nursing homes and providers of long-term home and personal care face the biggest cuts, hurting New York City disproportionately. Patients would be shifted to more costly levels of care, as those who now rely heavily on home attendant services would have to go to nursing homes. Adopting a new regional average cost method would give the city's nursing homes an operating deficit of $190 million.

--Reducing Tuition Assitance Program grants by $175 million would force City University of New York (CUNY) students to bear 41 percent of the cut, though city students, whose tuition is 12 percent higher thanthe national average, only get 25 percent of the aid. CUNY sees the reduction causing it to lose 12,000 students and forcing it to reduce services, faculty, and courses, and increase class sizes. But raising the number of hours professors teach could cut the need to raise tuition by saving $13.4 million in the first year.

--Welfare change could impose greater costs if they do not make recipients economically independent--a goal many may not be able to accomplish before they reach the new federal five-year limit on benefits. Over half of the city welfare recipients have gotten benefits for over four years, a much higher rate than for the nation as a whole, where only one in four are in that category.

Training programs will be cut to 45,000 in fiscal 1997, down from 58,000 in fiscal 1996. New York City does not create enough jobs for people without skills as fast as the rest of the country. Some neighborhoods, like six community districts in the Bronx, where more than 40 percent of the residents get public aid, will be hit particularly hard, hurting merchants and landlords too.
And Pataki wants to end "Jiggets" rent supplements for families that got eviction notices. If only 10 percent of these recipients go to homeless shelters, the city loses money.
